author: The Fence Line
title: The Remodel Was Half Done When They Fired the Builder, Then He Moved to Sell the House. A Texas Court Took His Claim Off It.
text:
1 days ago A couple relocating from California with five children bought a house in Austin that needed substantial remodeling before the family could fit. An interior decorator they hired recommended a builder, and on November 10, 2000, the wife signed the remodeling contract. Her husband did not, and that missing signature decided everything after.
Several months in, the couple decided the work was unacceptable and terminated the contract. The builder said his work was substantially complete and he was owed $42,897.66 for labor and materials. The couple said it would take $90,000 to fix damage he had caused.
The builder recorded mechanic's liens on the Travis County property. The contract carried an arbitration clause, and after a three-day hearing the arbitrator awarded him most of what he asked for and the couple nothing. Back in district court he asked to have the award confirmed and the liens foreclosed — in Texas, a judgment ordering the property sold. The couple answered that the house had been their homestead since the day they bought it, which would make the liens void.
What each side claimed The builder's argument was about timing. The family had claimed its California home as a homestead for seven years, and when the contract was signed the wife and five children were still there while the husband rented an Austin apartment. So, he argued, the Austin house was not yet a homestead.
The couple pointed to what they had already done. Court records show they had by then registered to vote and voted in Austin, obtained Texas driver's licenses, shipped and registered their car in Texas, and opened a joint checking account listing the house as their address. The wife and the decorator both testified she told the builder it was to be the family's permanent home; a representative of the builder testified this was never relayed to him.
It was undisputed that the builder had not followed the procedures Texas requires for a lien on a homestead, so homestead status alone decided the liens.
What Texas law actually says Section 53.254 of the Property Code sets five conditions before a contractor can fix a lien on a homestead: a written contract executed by the owner and the person furnishing labor or materials; executed before any material is furnished or labor performed; signed by both spouses if the owner is married; inuring to the benefit of everyone working under an original contractor; and filed with the county clerk where the homestead sits.
The third condition failed. The court noted the Texas Constitution sets the same rule: the agreement must be "in writing, with the consent of both spouses, in the case of a family homestead."
Timing did the rest. Homestead status is measured on the date the contract is signed, not the date anyone moves in, and a house can qualify before it is occupied: "Absent actual occupancy or intent to occupy coupled with overt acts of preparation evidencing that intention, no homestead right attaches," the court wrote, quoting a 1936 decision.
How it was resolved The 261st District Court in Travis County vacated the arbitration award, removed the liens, and set the couple's attorney's fees at $23,000.
On August 12, 2004, on rehearing, the Third Court of Appeals in Austin split the result three ways. It reinstated the arbitration award, holding the couple had waived their objection to the arbitrator by learning of his stock losses a month before the award and saying nothing until it went against them. It reversed the $23,000 in fees for want of evidence. And it affirmed that the liens were invalid: the house was the family's homestead when the contract was signed, and only one spouse had signed it.
The debt survived; the claim on the house did not. The Supreme Court of Texas denied review on February 11, 2005 and rehearing on May 6, 2005; the mandate issued May 13, 2005.
Before you sign a remodeling contract One signature was the whole case. Both sides agreed the contract failed the homestead lien rules, and the first reason given was that only one spouse had signed. The contract date controlled, not the move-in date. Homestead status was measured as of November 10, 2000, when most of the family was still out of state. Preparation counted without occupancy. Voter registration, driver's licenses and a checking account listing the house carried the finding. Telling the builder mattered. Testimony that the owner said before signing that it would be the family's home was treated as supporting evidence. Losing the lien is not losing the debt.
